title: AI Strategist: Fundamentals and Literacy
description: Domain 1 (24%): AI, ML and generative AI in business terms, data, choosing rules or AI, agents, shadow AI, prompting and model adaptation at a decision level.

cards.definition: The algorithm is the learning method; the model is what it produces after training on data, and the model is what a business uses to make predictions.
A model's output for new input: a likely answer with some chance of being wrong, not a guaranteed fact, so processes must allow for errors.

example.text: A fraud model scores a card payment as probably fraudulent. Because the score is a likelihood, not proof, the bank sends it for a quick check instead of closing the account.

cards.term: AI vs. ML vs. generative AI
cards.definition: AI is the umbrella; machine learning is the branch that learns from data instead of fixed instructions; generative AI, inside deep learning, creates new content.
Patterns in pre-defined data point to traditional ML; varied natural-language input or new content points to GenAI; multi-step goals point to agentic AI.

example.text: A retailer uses traditional ML to forecast demand, generative AI to draft product descriptions, and an agentic assistant to plan and book multi-step business trips.

cards.definition: Data that fits neatly into tables with a fixed format, such as numbers, short text and dates; the easiest kind to search and analyze.
Data that doesn't fit a table, such as long documents, audio, video and chat transcripts; making use of it usually takes ML or other AI.
AI results depend on the data behind them: missing values, inconsistent entries and noise all lower accuracy.
Data that reflects the full range of real users and cases; groups that are under-represented in it tend to get less accurate, less fair results.
A model trained on past records learns their patterns, including old bias, so it can carry yesterday's decisions into today.

example.text: A screening model trained on years of past hiring data keeps favouring the profile the company used to hire, even after hiring policy has changed.

cards.definition: Examples tagged with the right answer (such as 'fraud' or 'genuine') that supervised models learn from; labeling large volumes takes real effort.
The international standard for an AI management system (AIMS) that an organization can be certified against; AWS holding it does not certify its customers.
A framework standard that describes the parts of a generic AI system using machine learning and what each part does, so teams describe ML systems the same way.
Guidance on AI system impact assessments: how to judge an AI system's effects on people, groups and society, and fit that into existing risk reviews.
Automation that follows explicit steps and conditions set in advance; it is deterministic and easy to audit, so it suits tasks whose rules can be written down.
Before choosing AI, ask whether the problem can be solved by writing down a clear, compact set of rules; if it can, rules or ordinary software may be better.

example.text: Checking whether two images are identical needs only a few simple rules. Deciding whether two face photos show the same person can't be written as compact rules, so it needs AI.

cards.term: Agentic AI vs. traditional AI vs. software agents
cards.definition: Traditional AI predicts or classifies; software agents follow rules within set bounds; agentic AI takes a delegated goal and plans, acts and adapts.
Humans set the goal and the agent chooses the steps itself, such as deciding whether it can resolve a customer query or must hand it to a person.
Agents communicating, coordinating and sharing tasks with each other (and with people), so specialist agents can split a larger workflow between them instead of one agent doing it all.
Rule-based orchestration runs steps developers define, which is predictable and auditable; AI-native orchestration lets agents plan the steps from intent and context.
AWS names four: fully autonomous, human in the loop, co-pilot, and human-led with agent support; the higher the risk, the more the human leads.

example.text: A firm lets an agent route documents fully on its own, but for investment decisions the agent only recommends and a person makes the final call.

cards.definition: Unlike regular software, an AI application can get worse over time through data drift, concept drift and changing user expectations, so it must be actively managed.
Record how the system really performs in production, then flag when results move away from that baseline so owners can retrain or fix it.
Staff using AI tools the organization hasn't approved, often consumer apps, so company data leaves without oversight; outright bans tend to make it worse.

example.text: Staff paste customer notes into a free chatbot because the company tool is slow. The company launches one approved summarizer with single sign-on, then blocks the free tool.

cards.definition: A sanctioned tool staff may use for stated tasks and data; making it the easiest path is the main way to draw people away from shadow tools.
A tool staff may not use, typically a high-risk consumer app; block it only once an approved alternative is live, so people have somewhere to go.
A tool still going through security, privacy and procurement review, which can take a long time; it isn't approved for use until that review is done.
A clear task instruction, context about the domain, a few examples of the output wanted, and the input to work on; vague prompts get vague answers.
Prompt engineering is trial and error: check the output, adjust wording, context or examples, and repeat until the results are what you need.
What a business notices when input outgrows a model's context window: earlier parts of a long document or chat get ignored and answers drift off target.
Long documents, long chat histories and long answers each raise the cost of a GenAI request, because both input and output tokens are billed.
The quality of the data feeding a live model slips (more missing values, inconsistent entries or noise), so results decline quietly; alerts let owners retrain, audit upstream systems or fix the data.
The model looks up your current, authoritative documents when it answers, so it can use company facts without being retrained.
Retraining a model on thousands of labeled examples to change its tone, format or task behaviour; worth it only when prompting and RAG fall short.
